title: VII. Mitya’s Great Secret. Received With Hisses
paragraphs: “Gentlemen,” he began, as agitated as before, “I want to confess everything. That money was _my own_.” The lawyers’ faces dropped. This was not at all what they had expected.
“What do you mean?” Nikolay Parfenovitch stammered. “Earlier that same day, at five o’clock, you yourself told us—”

“Damn five o’clock that day, and damn what I told you! That has nothing to do with it now! That money was mine, my own, that is, stolen by me ... not mine, I mean, but stolen by me, fifteen hundred roubles, and I had it on me the whole time, the whole time ...”
“But where did you get it?”

“I took it off my neck, gentlemen, off this very neck ... it was right here, hanging round my neck, sewn up in a rag. I’d worn it a long time, a month, since the day I hung it there ... to my shame and disgrace!”
“And who was it you ... appropriated it from?”
“You mean ‘stole it’? Say it straight, now. Yes, I as good as stole it. But if you like, I ‘appropriated’ it. In my own mind I stole it. And last night I finished stealing it.”
“Last night? But you just said it was a month ago that you ... got hold of it?...”

“Yes. But not from my father. Not from my father, don’t worry. I didn’t steal it from my father, I stole it from her. Let me tell you without breaking in. It’s hard enough, you know. A month ago Katerina Ivanovna sent for me, the lady who used to be my betrothed. Do you know her?”
“Yes, of course.”
“I know you do. She’s a noble creature, the noblest of the noble. But she’s hated me for ever so long, oh, for ever so long ... and she had every reason to hate me, every reason!”
“Katerina Ivanovna!” Nikolay Parfenovitch cried out in astonishment. The prosecutor stared as well.

“Oh, don’t speak her name so lightly! I’m a scoundrel for dragging her in. Yes, I saw that she hated me ... for a long while.... Right from the start, even that evening at my lodging ... but enough, enough. You aren’t worthy even to hear about that. There’s no need for it at all.... All I need say is that a month ago she sent for me and gave me three thousand roubles to post to her sister and another relative in Moscow (as if she couldn’t have posted it herself!), and I ... it came just at the fatal moment of my life when I ... well, when I had just fallen in love with another woman, with her, with Grushenka, who’s sitting downstairs right now. I carried her off to Mokroe here, and in two days I blew half of that cursed three thousand, but the other half I kept on me. And I kept that half, that fifteen hundred, hung round my neck like a locket, until yesterday, when I undid it and spent it. What’s left of it, eight hundred roubles, is in your hands now, Nikolay Parfenovitch. That’s the change from the fifteen hundred I had yesterday.”
“One moment. How can that be? When you were here a month ago you spent three thousand, not fifteen hundred. Everybody knows it.”
“Who knows it? Who counted the money? Did I let anybody count it?”
“But you told everyone yourself that you’d spent exactly three thousand.”

“That’s true, I did. I said so to the whole town, and the whole town said so too. Even here in Mokroe everyone figured it was three thousand. But I didn’t spend three thousand. I spent fifteen hundred. The other fifteen hundred I sewed into a little bag. That’s how it was, gentlemen. That’s where yesterday’s money came from....”
“This is nearly miraculous,” Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.
“Let me ask you something,” the prosecutor said at last. “Had you told anyone at all about this before, I mean that you had fifteen hundred left on you a month ago?”
“I told nobody.”
“That is odd. Do you mean literally nobody?”
“Literally nobody. Not a soul.”

“Why were you so reticent? Why did you make such a secret of it? To put it more exactly: you have now told us your secret, which you yourself call ‘disgraceful.’ Yet in reality—comparatively speaking, of course—this act, the taking of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and only for a time, naturally, is in my view merely extreme recklessness, and not so disgraceful, given your character.... Grant that it was highly discreditable. Still, discreditable is not ‘disgraceful.’... Many people have guessed during this last month that you spent Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand, and I heard the tale myself, quite apart from your confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for one, had heard it as well, so that it was hardly a tale any more, just the gossip of the whole town. There are also signs, if I am not mistaken, that you admitted this yourself to somebody, I mean that the money was Katerina Ivanovna’s. So I am greatly surprised that up to this moment you have made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you say you set aside, and have, apparently, attached a feeling of positive horror to that secret.... It is hard to believe that confessing it could cost you such anguish.... Just now you cried out that Siberia would be better than confessing it ...”

The prosecutor broke off. He was irritated. He made no effort to hide his vexation, which was close to anger, and he poured out all his stored-up bile in a scattered, tangled way, without picking his words.
“The disgrace isn’t the fifteen hundred. It’s that I kept it apart from the rest of the three thousand,” Mitya said firmly.

“Why?” the prosecutor smiled sourly. “What is disgraceful, to your mind, in setting aside half of the three thousand you had taken discreditably, or ‘disgracefully’ if you prefer? That you took the three thousand matters more than what you did with it. And by the way, why did you do it—why did you put that half aside, for what purpose, with what aim? Can you explain that to us?”

“Oh, gentlemen, the purpose is the whole point!” Mitya cried. “I set it aside because I was vile, that is, because I was calculating, and calculating in such a case is vile ... and that vileness has lasted a whole month.”
“I can’t make sense of it.”

“You amaze me. But I’ll put it more clearly. Maybe it really is hard to follow. Now listen carefully. Say I take three thousand entrusted to my honor and blow it on a spree, say I blow all of it, and next morning I go to her and say, ‘Katya, I did wrong, I’ve squandered your three thousand.’ Well, is that right? No, it isn’t right. It’s dishonest and cowardly. I’m a beast, no better at holding myself back than a beast, that’s so, isn’t it? But I’m still not a thief, am I? Not an out-and-out thief, you’ll grant me that! I squandered it, I didn’t steal it. Now the second case, a little more favorable. Follow me closely, or I’ll get muddled again, my head’s going round. In the second case I spend only fifteen hundred of the three thousand here, only half. The next day I take that half to her and say, ‘Katya, take this fifteen hundred from me. I’m a low beast and a scoundrel you can’t trust, because I’ve wasted half the money, and I’ll waste this too, so save me from temptation!’ Well, what about that case? I’d be a beast and a scoundrel, whatever you like, but not a thief, not altogether a thief. If I were, I wouldn’t have brought back what was left, I’d have kept that too. She would see at once that since I’d brought back half, I would pay back what I’d spent, that I’d never stop trying, that I’d work for it and pay it back. So then I’d be a scoundrel, but not a thief, say what you please, not a thief!”
“I grant that there is a certain distinction,” the prosecutor said with a cold smile. “It is odd, though, that you see such a vital difference.”

“Yes, I see a vital difference! Any man can be a scoundrel, and perhaps every man is one, but not everyone can be a thief. For that you have to be an arch-scoundrel. Oh, of course, I don’t know how to draw these fine lines ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that’s what I believe. Listen: I carry the money on me for a whole month. I might make up my mind tomorrow to give it back, and then I’m not a scoundrel anymore. But I can’t make up my mind, you see, though I decide every day, every day I push myself to do it, and still for a whole month I can’t bring myself to it. Is that right, do you think? Is that right?”

“Certainly it isn’t right. I understand that perfectly well, and I don’t dispute it,” the prosecutor answered stiffly. “Let us drop all discussion of these subtleties and distinctions and, if you would be so good, return to the point. And the point is this: you have still not told us—and we have asked—why in the first place you divided the money, squandering one half and hiding the other. What exactly was your purpose in hiding it? What did you intend to do with that fifteen hundred? I insist on that question, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Yes, of course!” Mitya cried, striking his forehead. “Forgive me, I’m tiring you out and not explaining the main thing, otherwise you’d understand at once, because it’s the motive itself that’s the disgrace! You see, it all had to do with the old man, my dead father. He was forever after Agrafena Alexandrovna, and I was jealous. In those days I thought she was wavering between him and me. So every day I kept thinking: what if she suddenly makes up her mind, what if she stops tormenting me and says, ‘I love you, not him. Take me to the other end of the world.’ And all I had was forty kopecks. How could I take her away, what could I do? I’d be done for. You see, I didn’t know her then, I didn’t understand her. I thought she wanted money, and that she wouldn’t forgive me for being poor. So, devil that I was, I counted out half of that three thousand and sewed it up, counting on it, sewed it up while I was still sober. And once it was sewn up, I went off to get drunk on the rest. Yes, that was base. Do you understand now?”
Both lawyers burst out laughing.
“I would have called it sensible and moral of you not to squander everything,” Nikolay Parfenovitch chuckled. “After all, what does it come to?”

“It comes to this, that I stole it! Oh, God, it horrifies me that you don’t understand! Every day I had that fifteen hundred sewn up round my neck, every day and every hour I told myself, ‘You’re a thief! You’re a thief!’ That’s why I’ve been so savage all this month. That’s why I fought in the tavern, that’s why I attacked my father: because I felt I was a thief. I couldn’t make up my mind. I didn’t dare even to tell Alyosha, my own brother, about that fifteen hundred. I felt like such a scoundrel and such a pickpocket. But you know, while I carried it I also told myself every hour, ‘No, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, you might still turn out not to be a thief.’ Why? Because next day I could go and pay that fifteen hundred back to Katya. And only yesterday I made up my mind to rip the amulet off my neck, on my way from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s. Until then I hadn’t been able to bring myself to do it. And the moment I tore it off, I became a downright thief, a thief and a dishonest man for the rest of my life. Why? Because with that I destroyed my dream, too, of going to Katya and saying, ‘I’m a scoundrel, but not a thief!’ Do you understand now? Do you understand?”
“What made you decide to do it yesterday?” Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in.

“Why? What a ridiculous question. Because I’d sentenced myself to die at five o’clock this morning, here, at dawn. I thought it made no difference whether I died a thief or an honorable man. But I see it isn’t so. It turns out it does make a difference. Believe me, gentlemen, what tortured me most this night wasn’t the thought that I’d killed the old servant, or that Siberia was hanging over me just when my love was being rewarded and Heaven was open to me again. Oh, that tortured me, but not like this. Not as much as the cursed knowledge that I’d finally torn that cursed money off my chest and spent it, and become a downright thief! Oh, gentlemen, I tell you again, with a bleeding heart, I’ve learned a great deal this night. I’ve learned that you can’t live as a scoundrel, and you can’t die as one either.... No, gentlemen, a man must die honest....”
Mitya was pale. For all his fierce excitement, his face looked haggard and worn out.

“I am beginning to understand you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said slowly, in a soft and almost sympathetic tone. “But all of this, if you’ll forgive my saying so, is in my opinion a matter of nerves ... overwrought nerves, that is what it is. Why, for example, did you not spare yourself nearly a month of such misery by going and returning that fifteen hundred to the lady who had entrusted it to you? And why could you not have explained matters to her? Given your position, which you describe as so dreadful, why did you not turn to the remedy that would occur so naturally to anyone? After honestly confessing your mistakes to her, why did you not ask her to lend you the money you needed? With her generous heart she would surely not have refused you in your distress, particularly if you had offered some guarantee, or even the same security you offered the merchant Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. I suppose you still consider that security to be worth something?”
Mitya suddenly went crimson.
“Surely you don’t take me for such an out-and-out scoundrel as that? You can’t be serious!” he said indignantly. He stared the prosecutor straight in the face, as if he couldn’t believe his ears.
“I assure you I am serious.... Why would you think I’m not?” Now it was the prosecutor’s turn to be surprised.

“Oh, how low that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you’re torturing me! All right, I’ll tell you everything. I’ll confess all my infernal wickedness, but only to put you to shame. You’ll be amazed yourselves at the depths of disgrace a jumble of human passions can sink to. You should know that I had that plan myself, the one you just mentioned, prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, that thought has been in my head all this month too. I was on the point of deciding to go to Katya—I was mean enough for that. But to go to her, to tell her about my treachery, and for that very treachery, to carry it out, to pay for that treachery, to beg money from her, from Katya (to beg, do you hear, to beg), and go straight from her to run away with the other woman, her rival, who hated her and insulted her—to think of it! You must be mad, prosecutor!”

“I’m not mad, but I spoke in haste, without thinking ... about that feminine jealousy ... if there could be any jealousy in this case, as you claim ... yes, perhaps there is something of the kind,” said the prosecutor, smiling.

“But that would have been so infamous!” Mitya brought his fist down fiercely on the table. “It would have been filthier than anything! Do you know, she might have given me that money? Yes, she would have given it; she’d certainly have given it, out of revenge, to satisfy her vengeance, to show me her contempt. She has an infernal nature too, and she’s a woman of great wrath. I’d have taken it, oh yes, I’d have taken the money; I’d have taken it, and then for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I’m shouting like this because the thought has been in my mind so recently, only the day before yesterday, that night when I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then all day yesterday, I remember, right up until that happened ...”
“Until what happened?” put in Nikolay Parfenovitch curiously, but Mitya did not hear.

“I’ve made you a terrible confession,” Mitya concluded gloomily. “You must appreciate it, and what’s more, you must respect it. If you don’t, if it leaves your souls untouched, then you simply have no respect for me, gentlemen, I tell you that. I’ll die of shame at having confessed it to men like you! Oh, I’ll shoot myself! Yes, I see, I can see already that you don’t believe me. What, you want to write that down too?” he cried in dismay.

“Yes, what you just said,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, looking at him in surprise. “That is, that right up to the last hour you were still thinking of going to Katerina Ivanovna to beg that sum from her.... I assure you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, that is a very important piece of evidence for us, for the whole case, I mean ... and especially for you, especially important for you.”

“Have mercy, gentlemen!” Mitya threw up his hands. “At least don’t write that down; have some shame. I’ve torn my heart in two in front of you, and you seize the chance to poke at the wounds in both halves.... Oh, my God!”
In despair he buried his face in his hands.

“Don’t upset yourself so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor said. “Everything we write down will be read back to you afterwards, and whatever you don’t agree with we’ll change as you wish. But now I’ll ask you one small question for the second time. Did no one, absolutely no one, ever hear from you about that money you sewed up? I must tell you, that is almost impossible to believe.”
“No one, no one! I told you so already, or else you haven’t understood a thing! Leave me alone!”

“Very well. This matter is bound to be cleared up, and there’s plenty of time for that. But meanwhile, consider this. We have perhaps a dozen witnesses that you spread it around yourself, even shouted it almost everywhere, that you’d spent three thousand here. Three thousand, not fifteen hundred. And just now too, when you got hold of the money you had yesterday, you let many people understand that you’d brought three thousand with you.”
“You don’t have dozens of witnesses, you have hundreds! Two hundred witnesses, two hundred people heard it, thousands heard it!” cried Mitya.
“Well, you see, they all bear witness to it. And that word _all_ means something.”
“It means nothing. I talked rot, and everyone started repeating it.”
“But why did you need to ‘talk rot,’ as you put it?”

“The devil knows. Out of bravado, perhaps ... at having wasted so much money.... Or to try to forget the money I’d sewn up, perhaps ... yes, that was why ... damn it ... how many times are you going to ask me that? Well, I told a fib, and that was that. Once I’d said it, I couldn’t be bothered to take it back. Why does a man tell lies sometimes?”

“That’s very hard to say, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, why a man tells lies,” the prosecutor observed impressively. “Tell me, though, was that ‘amulet’ you wore around your neck, as you call it, a big thing?”
“No, not big.”
“How big, for instance?”
“Fold a hundred-rouble note in half, and that’s about the size.”
“You’d better show us what’s left of it. You must have it somewhere.”
“Damnation, what nonsense! I don’t know where it is.”
“But excuse me, where and when did you take it off your neck? By your own account you never went home.”
“I tore it off my neck on the way from Fenya’s to Perhotin’s, and took out the money.”
“In the dark?”
“What would I want a light for? I did it with my fingers in a minute.”
“Without scissors, in the street?”
“In the market-place, I think it was. Why scissors? It was an old rag. It tore in a minute.”
“And where did you put it afterwards?”
“I dropped it there.”
“Where, exactly?”
“In the market-place, in the market-place! The devil knows where. What do you want to know for?”
“It’s extremely important, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. It would be material evidence in your favor. How is it you can’t see that? Who helped you sew it up a month ago?”
“No one helped me. I did it myself.”
“Can you sew?”
“A soldier has to know how to sew. It took no skill at all.”
“And where did you get the material, that is, the rag you sewed the money into?”
“Are you laughing at me?”
“Not at all. And we’re in no mood for laughing, Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”
“I don’t know where I got the rag from—somewhere, I suppose.”
“I would have thought you couldn’t possibly have forgotten that?”
“Honestly, I don’t remember. I may have torn a piece off my linen.”
“That’s very interesting. Tomorrow we might find, at your lodgings, the shirt or whatever it is that you tore the rag from. What sort of rag was it, cloth or linen?”
“Goodness only knows what it was. Wait a bit.... I don’t think I tore it off anything. It was a bit of calico.... I think I sewed it up in a cap of my landlady’s.”
“In your landlady’s cap?”
“Yes. I took it from her.”
“How did you come by it?”

“Well, I remember once picking up a cap to use as a rag, maybe to wipe my pen on. I took it without asking, since it was a worthless rag. I tore it up, then took the notes and sewed them into it. I think it was in that very rag that I sewed them. An old piece of calico, washed a thousand times.”
“And you remember that for certain now?”
“I don’t know about for certain. I think it was the cap. But, hang it, what does it matter?”
“In that case your landlady will remember that her cap went missing?”
“No, she won’t. She never missed it. It was an old rag, I tell you, an old rag not worth a farthing.”
“And where did you get the needle and thread?”
“That’s it, I’m stopping. I won’t say another word. Enough of this!” said Mitya, losing his temper at last.
“It’s odd that you should have forgotten so completely where you threw the pieces in the market-place.”

“Have the market-place swept tomorrow, and perhaps you’ll find it,” Mitya sneered. “Enough, gentlemen, enough!” he decided in an exhausted voice. “I see you don’t believe me! Not for a moment! The fault is mine, not yours. I shouldn’t have been so quick to talk. Why, why did I lower myself by confessing my secret to you? It’s a joke to you. I can see it in your eyes. You led me into it, prosecutor! Go on, sing your hymn of triumph if you can.... Damn you, you torturers!”

He bowed his head and hid his face in his hands. The lawyers said nothing. A minute later he looked up at them with an almost vacant stare. His face now showed complete, hopeless despair. He sat mute and passive, hardly aware of what was going on. Meanwhile the others had to finish their business. They had to begin examining the witnesses at once. It was already eight o’clock in the morning. The lamps had been put out long before. Mihail Makarovitch and Kalganov, who had been in and out of the room all through the interrogation, had both left again. The lawyers too looked very tired. It was a wretched morning. The whole sky was overcast, and the rain came down in buckets. Mitya gazed blankly out of the window.
“Can I look out of the window?” he suddenly asked Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Oh, look as much as you like,” the latter replied.

Mitya got up and went to the window.... The rain lashed at its little greenish panes. Just below the house he could see the muddy road, and farther off, through rain and mist, a row of poor, black, dismal huts that looked even blacker and poorer in the wet. Mitya thought of “Phœbus the golden-haired,” and how he had meant to shoot himself at his first ray. “Maybe it would be even better on a morning like this,” he thought with a smile. Then he suddenly swung his arm down and turned to his “torturers.”

“Gentlemen,” he cried, “I see I’m lost! But what about her? Tell me about her, I beg you. Surely she doesn’t have to be ruined along with me? She’s innocent, you know. She was out of her mind when she cried last night, ‘It’s all my fault!’ She’s done nothing, nothing! I’ve been grieving over her all night, sitting here with you.... Can’t you tell me, won’t you tell me, what you’re going to do with her now?”

“On that score you can set your mind completely at rest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” the prosecutor answered at once, with obvious eagerness. “So far we have no grounds for troubling the lady you take such an interest in. I trust it will stay that way as the case develops.... On the contrary, we’ll do everything in our power on that point. Set your mind entirely at rest.”
“Gentlemen, thank you. I knew you were honest, straightforward men, in spite of everything. You’ve lifted a weight from my heart.... Well, what do we do now? I’m ready.”
“Well, we ought to hurry. We have to go on to the witnesses without delay. That must be done in your presence, and therefore—”
“Shouldn’t we have some tea first?” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. “I think we’ve earned it!”

They agreed that if tea was ready downstairs (Mihail Makarovitch had no doubt gone down to fetch some), they would have a glass and then “go on and on,” leaving their proper breakfast for a better time. Tea really was ready below, and was soon brought up. At first Mitya turned down the glass that Nikolay Parfenovitch politely offered him, but then he asked for it himself and drank it greedily. He looked astonishingly worn out. With his Herculean strength, you might have thought that one night of carousing, even with the most violent emotions thrown in, would have done him little harm. But he felt he could hardly hold his head up, and from time to time everything around him seemed to heave and dance before his eyes. “A little more and I’ll start raving,” he said to himself.
